items.title: Leaf The Lake Alone! Ameren Warns Against Dumping Fall Leaves Into Lake Of The Ozarks
items.desc: Fall leaves may look harmless, but piles of them pushed into Lake of the Ozarks can create real problems for water quality.
items.body: Fall leaves may look harmless, but piles of them pushed into Lake of the Ozarks can create real problems for water quality. Residents, property owners, and lawn crews are being encouraged not to blow, dump, or push leaves and other yard waste into the Lake. Instead, Ameren Missouri recommends mulching, composting, or using an approved disposal service. Leaves that fall naturally into the Lake are part of its ecosystem. Problems can arise, however, when concentrated piles are intentionally pushed into the water. As that material decomposes, it can release nutrients, contribute to algae growth, and use oxygen needed by fish and other aquatic life. "When leaves are blown into a cove, they don't just disappear," said Bryan Vance, manager of shoreline management at Ameren Missouri. "As those leaves break down, they can affect water quality and create issues along the shoreline. Taking a few extra minutes to mulch, compost or properly dispose of leaves can make a real difference." - Mulch leaves. Run over leaves with a mower and use them around trees, shrubs, and garden beds to help retain moisture and suppress weeds. - Start or add to a compost pile. Combine leaves with grass clippings and food scraps to create nutrient-rich compost. - Bag and dispose of leaves properly. Check with local waste services, municipalities or landscaping companies for collection and composting options. If you hire a lawn service, ask how it disposes of collected leaves. Commercial landscaping and lawn care companies are prohibited from disposing of leaves and other yard waste in Missouri's public waters. - Burn only where permitted. items.title: The Shroud Of Turin: Free Lake Area Exhibit Explores Its History & Mysteries
items.desc: LAURIE, Mo. — A traveling exhibit exploring the history, science, and religious significance of the Shroud of Turin is coming to the National Shrine of Mary, Mother of the Church, in Laurie this month.
items.body: LAURIE, Mo. — A traveling exhibit exploring the history, science, and religious significance of the Shroud of Turin is coming to the National Shrine of Mary, Mother of the Church, in Laurie this month. “Who is the Man of the Shroud?” will feature a replica of the Shroud of Turin, along with interpretive panels examining the cloth’s documented history, physical characteristics, scientific study, and connections to Gospel accounts of the Passion and burial of Jesus. The exhibit, being displayed Nov. 5-15, is presented by Shroud Exhibitors of Central Missouri in partnership with Othonia, Inc. Visitors will also be able to scan QR codes for an audio guide, quick facts, and additional educational resources. “We are truly excited to welcome the Shroud of Turin exhibit to the National Shrine of Mary, Mother of the Church,” said Andrew Wright, executive director of the Shrine. “The Shroud invites us to reflect on Christ’s suffering and sacrifice, the depth of His love for humanity, and the hope of His Resurrection.” The exhibit is intended for visitors of all ages and faith backgrounds and will be available free of charge, with donations encouraged to support Shroud Exhibitors of Central Missouri. The National Shrine of Mary, Mother of the Church is located at 176 Marian Drive in Laurie. The Shrine, also known as the Mothers’ Shrine, serves as a place for prayer, pilgrimage, and reflection and includes the Mothers’ Wall of Life and a large sculpture of Mary. - Wednesday through Friday: 10 a.m.–1 p.m. Visitors are encouraged to check mothersshrine.com or the Shrine’s Facebook page for current hours and additional information.

items.title: Needles In Halloween Candy? Sheriff Offers Free X-Rays After Lake Area Woman Says She Found Some
items.desc: CAMDEN COUNTY, Mo. — The Camden County Sheriff's Office is offering free X-Rays of kids' Halloween candy, after receiving a report from a local woman who said needles were found in her grandkids' treats.
items.body: CAMDEN COUNTY, Mo. — The Camden County Sheriff's Office is offering free X-Rays of kids' Halloween candy, after receiving a report from a local woman who said needles were found in her grandkids' treats. ATTENTION: Last night, Halloween, deputies took a confirmed report of a family finding needles in a piece of Halloween candy. This family was trick-or-treating in the HH area of Camden County. While the investigation into the source of the candy continues we would like to invite anyone concerned about the safety of their Halloween candy to bring it to the Camden County Justice Center for an X-ray. While the Justice Center is closed on Sundays we are opening the doors today from 11:00am to 2:00pm for anyone who wants to bring their candy in for inspection. We will also make this service available throughout this week during regular business hours. We have no information indicating this is anything more than an isolated incident but, out of an abundance of caution, we encourage anyone concerned to come to the Justice Center. The woman who made the report — a local schoolteacher named Sarah Stoufer — said her grandchildren had been trick-or-treating in the neighborhood on Palmer Road off Route HH, an extremely popular trick-or-treating location annually at the Lake. The sheriff's office says it was still investigating the source of the candy, but offered free X-Rays this week for anyone who wanted their children's candy checked. On Halloween night, the Hickory County, Missouri sheriff's office also announced they received a report of a Payday candy bar with a straight-pin inside it.

items.title: Camden County Water District Gets $223K For Drinking Water Upgrades
items.desc: CAMDEN COUNTY, Mo. — Camden County Public Water Supply District No. 5 has received a $223,000 interest-free loan from the Missouri Department of Natural Resources to help plan and design future drinking water system improvements.
items.body: CAMDEN COUNTY, Mo. — Camden County Public Water Supply District No. 5 has received a $223,000 interest-free loan from the Missouri Department of Natural Resources to help plan and design future drinking water system improvements. The funding comes through the department’s Planning and Design Loan Program and will cover early engineering and administrative costs while the district works toward a larger construction funding package. The district estimates the full improvement project will cost about $3 million, with construction expected to begin in 2028. According to DNR, the planning loan carries no interest and has a five-year term. The department estimates that will save local ratepayers about $48,000 in interest compared with other financing options. “Investing in local water infrastructure is not just about improving drinking water systems; it’s about revitalizing communities and ensuring residents have access to abundant, safe drinking water,” said Jake Buxton, director of the Missouri Department of Natural Resources. The larger project could eventually qualify for additional financing through Missouri’s Drinking Water State Revolving Fund, which supports improvements to water treatment plants, distribution systems, water storage, supply facilities, and other drinking water infrastructure. DNR said the Camden County project will be funded wholly or in part with money received from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. More information about Missouri drinking water and wastewater funding programs is available through the Department of Natural Resources’ State Revolving Fund program.

items.title: MHS Brings Back JROTC, Builds Tomorrow’s Leaders
items.desc: Marshfield High School’s Marine Corps JROTC program returns after a four-year effort, giving students a chance to learn practical skills, explore career options, and get involved in their community. The […]
items.body: Staff Sergeant Matthew Baker and Cayleb Cook (Photo provided by Breanne Rost) 2/2 Swipe or click to see more Screenshot_20261023_102810_Gmail%20(1).jpg (Photo provided by Breanne Rost) Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Marshfield High School’s Marine Corps JROTC program returns after a four-year effort, giving students a chance to learn practical skills, explore career options, and get involved in their community. The Junior Reserve Officers’ Training Corps, better known as JROTC, combines classroom instruction with military traditions, physical fitness, and community service. But joining the program doesn’t mean students have to pursue a military career. The goal is to help prepare them for whatever comes after high school. For Marshfield R-1 Superintendent Garrett Lowder, bringing the program back has been a priority for both the district and the community. “We had identified through our community feedback and our board that bringing JROTC back to Marshfield School District was something that was a high priority for us,” Lowder said. Marshfield previously offered JROTC, and school leaders spent roughly four years working to bring it back. The district even included space for the program in a new facility while waiting for approval. Now, two former Marines are helping get things started. Staff Sergeant Matthew Barker, who served nine years in the Marine Corps, and First Sergeant Joseph Bednarik, who retired in July after 23 years of active duty, are leading the program. While uniforms, marching, and military drills are part of JROTC, Barker says students can take much more from the experience. “Our entire curriculum is titled Leadership Education,” Barker explained. Marshfield Community Theatre Presents: Carrie: The Musical This Halloween
items.desc: This Halloween season, the Marshfield Community Theatre is bringing you something old and something new. “We are currently producing Carrie: The Musical, based on the iconic story by Stephen King,” […]
items.body: This Halloween season, the Marshfield Community Theatre is bringing you something old and something new. “We are currently producing Carrie: The Musical, based on the iconic story by Stephen King,” shared an excited Kelby Lorenz, Director of Carrie and Director of Outreach for Marshfield Community Theatre. “We chose this show because it’s October; we are doing it Halloween weekend. It seemed like a really good spooky show, but when I read the script, it tells a really incredible story,” reflected Lorenz. “One of the things that I love about this show and the way that it’s interpreted is that it’s a closed loop-we end where we start. We got to really play with the idea of how long have we been stuck in this loop…and how long have we been trying to stop the destruction.” “It’s a cool concept to play with-around the idea of trauma, how it stays with us…and how traumatic moments can really impact the way we interact with each other,” expressed Lorenz. “It really centers on that theme-what does it cost to be kind?” The cast includes around 16, with most actors new to MCT, including a mix of MSU students and brand-new actors. The production team includes Lorenz as Director, Nico Jenkins as Assistant Director, Linley Wilson as Music Director, Miliani Kloster as Choreographer, and Toni Lorenz as Production Manager. “It’s been super fun,” shared Lauren Knight, a Missouri State student playing Carrie White. “I haven’t done a lot of roles where I’m a lead- it’s been a bit of a change. It’s been fun to get to know this character. She’s been a bit of a challenge…I’ve learned to be more vulnerable on stage.
